name: Titans
note: Ouranos and Gaia's twelve, and what they fathered

Okeanos.name: Okeanos (Oceanus)
Okeanos.note: The river that runs round the rim of the world, eldest Titan, and the one who never fought Zeus. Gives ocean, oceanography. Theog. 133

Koios.name: Koios (Coeus)
Koios.note: Titan of the inquiring mind; grandfather of Apollo and Artemis through Leto. Theog. 134

Krios.name: Krios (Crius)
Krios.note: The ram; a Titan of whom little survives but his sons. Theog. 134

Hyperion.note: The one who goes above -- father of Sun, Moon and Dawn, and himself an older sun. Keats left an epic of his name unfinished twice. Theog. 134

Iapetos.name: Iapetos (Iapetus)
Iapetos.note: Father of Atlas and Prometheus, and so of mankind's troubles. Often compared to Japheth, son of Noah. Theog. 134

Theia.note: The divine one, mother of the lights of heaven. Theog. 135

Rheia.name: Rheia (Ops)
Rheia.note: Mother of the Olympians, who gave Kronos a swaddled stone to swallow instead of Zeus. Roman: Ops, whence opulent. Theog. 135, 453-491

Themis.name: Themis (Justitia)
Themis.note: Divine law -- what is laid down, as against nomos, what is enacted. Roman: Justitia, the blindfolded figure over courthouses. Theog. 135, 901-906

Mnemosyne.name: Mnemosyne (Moneta)
Mnemosyne.note: Memory, who lay with Zeus nine nights and bore the nine Muses. Gives mnemonic, amnesia, amnesty -- a decree to forget. Roman: Moneta, and because Rome's mint stood in her temple, that name gives money and mint both. Theog. 135, 915-917

Phoibe.name: Phoibe (Phoebe)
Phoibe.note: The bright one; her name passes to her grandson Apollo as Phoibos. Theog. 136

Tethys.note: Wife of Okeanos, mother of every river and three thousand daughters. The Tethys Ocean of geology, which lay between Gondwana and Laurasia, is named for her. Theog. 136

Kronos.name: Kronos (Saturn)
Kronos.note: Youngest and most terrible of the twelve: he cut his father with the sickle and ate his own children. Roman: Saturn, whose festival was the Saturnalia and whose day is Saturday -- the only day of the English week still named for a Roman god. FALSE FRIEND, worth stating plainly because everyone assumes it: Kronos the Titan and chronos, time, are NOT related. The identification is a late pun that hardened into folklore, and it is why Saturn carries a scythe and became Father Time. Theog. 137, 453-506

Brontes.note: One of the three Kyklopes, one-eyed smiths who forged Zeus' thunderbolt in return for their freedom. Thunder. Gives brontosaurus, the thunder lizard. Theog. 140

Steropes.note: One of the three Kyklopes, one-eyed smiths who forged Zeus' thunderbolt in return for their freedom. Lightning. Theog. 140

Arges.note: One of the three Kyklopes, one-eyed smiths who forged Zeus' thunderbolt in return for their freedom. Brightness. Theog. 140

Kottos.note: One of the three Hekatoncheires, hundred-handed and fifty-headed, who threw the rocks that buried the Titans. Theog. 149

Briareos.note: One of the three Hekatoncheires, hundred-handed and fifty-headed, who threw the rocks that buried the Titans. Called Aigaion by men and Briareos by the gods; Thetis fetched him to Olympos to sit beside Zeus and frighten the other gods off a rebellion. Theog. 149, Il. 1.401-406

Gyges.note: One of the three Hekatoncheires, hundred-handed and fifty-headed, who threw the rocks that buried the Titans. Theog. 149

Helios.name: Helios (Sol)
Helios.note: The Sun, who sees and hears everything and so is the witness called in oaths. Roman: Sol -- solar, solstice, parasol. From the Greek: helium, named in 1868 when it was found in the sun's spectrum before it was found on earth, and heliocentric, heliotrope, aphelion. Theog. 371

Selene.name: Selene (Luna)
Selene.note: The Moon, who drives a chariot of two horses. Roman: Luna -- lunar, lunatic, lunacy, from the belief that her light unsettled the mind. From the Greek: selenium, named by Berzelius in 1817 after the moon because it sat beside tellurium, named for the earth. Theog. 371

Eos.name: Eos (Aurora)
Eos.note: Dawn, rosy-fingered, who opens the gates for her brother. Roman: Aurora -- the aurora borealis is her northern light. From the Greek: eosin, the rose-coloured dye, and the Eocene epoch, the dawn of the modern. Theog. 371

Leto.name: Leto (Latona)
Leto.note: Mother of Apollo and Artemis by Zeus, and hounded over the whole earth by Hera, who forbade any land to receive her -- until floating Delos, which was no land, let her stop. Roman: Latona. Theog. 406

Asteria.note: The starry one, who turned herself into a quail and then into the island of Delos to escape Zeus -- and so became the one place her sister Leto could give birth. Gives asteroid, asterisk, disaster, which is literally an ill star. Theog. 409

Astraios.note: Titan of the stars of the dusk. Theog. 376

Pallas.note: Titan of warcraft, husband of Styx. Not Pallas Athena, who takes the name from a different story. Theog. 376

Perses.note: Titan of destruction, father of Hekate, and the one from whom the Persians were said to take their name. Theog. 377

Hekate.name: Hekate (Trivia)
Hekate.note: Goddess of the crossroads, of the boundary, and of witchcraft; Hesiod gives her a share of earth, sea and sky, which no other single deity holds. Roman: Trivia -- literally 'three roads', the place her shrines stood. That word gives English trivial, by way of the trivium, the three lower liberal arts, and the sense of what is talked about where three roads meet. Theog. 409-411

Boreas.name: Boreas (Aquilo)
Boreas.note: The north wind, cold and violent; he carried off Oreithyia of Athens. Gives boreal, aurora borealis, and the Hyperboreans, who lived beyond the north wind. Theog. 379

Notos.name: Notos (Auster)
Notos.note: The south wind, bringer of storm and late-summer rain. Roman: Auster, whence austral and Australia, the southern land. Theog. 380

Zephyros.name: Zephyros (Favonius)
Zephyros.note: The west wind, gentlest of them, who brings the spring. Gives zephyr. Theog. 379 He loved Hyakinthos too, and it was his jealousy that turned the discus.

Euros.name: Euros (Vulturnus)
Euros.note: The east wind, the unlucky one Hesiod does not list with his brothers. Cited rather than read in Hesiod; the fourfold set is later. Hyg. Fab. pref.

Eosphoros.name: Eosphoros (Lucifer)
Eosphoros.note: The Dawn-bringer, the morning star. Roman: Lucifer, the light-bearer -- the same star, and the name only became a devil's much later, when Jerome used it in Isaiah 14 for a fallen king of Babylon. Also Phosphoros, which gives the element phosphorus, named for glowing in the dark. Theog. 381

Nike.name: Nike (Victoria)
Nike.note: Victory. Roman: Victoria -- victor, victory. The Greek name is now a shoe, chosen in 1971 for exactly the reason it meant something in 480 BC. Theog. 384

Kratos.name: Kratos (Potestas)
Kratos.note: Strength, or rather power-over: the -cracy in democracy, aristocracy, autocrat. Theog. 385

Zelos.name: Zelos (Invidia)
Zelos.note: Rivalry, emulation. Gives zeal, zealot, jealous. Theog. 384

Atlas.note: Condemned to hold the sky apart from the earth at the western edge for ever -- not the globe, which is a Renaissance misreading. Gives atlas (a book of maps, from Mercator putting him on the frontispiece in 1595), the Atlantic ocean, the Atlas mountains, and the atlas vertebra, the top one, which holds up the head. Theog. 517-520

Prometheus.note: Forethought. He tricked Zeus over the sacrificial portions, stole fire back in a fennel stalk after Zeus hid it, and was chained to a rock for an eagle to eat his liver daily until Herakles shot it. Made mankind from clay in the later tradition. Gives Promethean, and promethium, element 61, named in 1945 for the theft of fire. Theog. 510-616

Epimetheus.note: Afterthought, the slow brother, who accepted Pandora from the gods against Prometheus' warning and so let the jar be opened. Theog. 511-514, WD 83-89

Menoitios.note: Struck down by Zeus' thunderbolt into Erebos for his violence and presumption. Theog. 514-516

Elektra3.name: Elektra
Elektra3.note: One of the seven Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, and mother of Dardanos by Zeus. The third Elektra in this tree -- the Okeanid and Agamemnon's daughter are the others. Apollod. 3.12.1

Maia.note: Eldest Pleiad, mother of Hermes in a cave on Kyllene. Roman: Maia, and MAY is her month. Hom. Hymn Herm. 1-9

Taygete.note: A Pleiad, daughter of Atlas, loved by Zeus; MOUNT TAYGETOS above Sparta is hers. Apollod. 3.10.1

unions.note: Eighteen children, and Ouranos hated every one: he hid them in Gaia's body as fast as they were born until she made the grey adamant sickle and Kronos took it. Theog. 132-153
Dawn lay with the god of the dusk stars and bore the winds and the morning star: the sky's whole daily traffic in one union. Theog. 378-382
Styx brought her four children to Olympos first of all the gods when Zeus called, and for that they stand beside his throne for ever and her water became the oath no god may break. Theog. 383-403
Theog. 507-511. Apollodoros makes the mother Asia rather than Klymene; both are Okeanids and the disagreement is old. Apollod. 1.2.3
The Pleiades, seven sisters set among the stars; the tree keeps the two whose sons matter. Apollod. 3.10.1, 3.12.1
She asked Zeus to keep him asleep and ageless, and came down to him nightly. Fifty daughters. Apollod. 1.7.5
Dawn carried him off, and Artemis shot him for it. Apollod. 1.4.4
